candidate.answerReason: The angle-bisector condition gives \(CA=OC\sin\theta\). Since \(CA+OC=1\), the requested length is \(1/(1+\sin\theta)\), agreeing with D.

methods.label: Equal distances from an angle bisector
methods.explanation:
The angle bisector is useful because every point on it has equal perpendicular distances to the two sides of the angle. Tangency gives \(OA\perp AB\), so triangle \(OAB\) is right and \(0<\theta<90^\circ\).

Let \(x=OC\). The internal bisector meets the interior of \(OA\), so \(0<x<1\) and \(CA=1-x\). Because \(CA\perp AB\), the distance from \(C\) to line \(AB\) is \(1-x\).

Draw \(CH\perp OB\), with \(H\) on \(OB\). In right triangle \(OCH\), the hypotenuse is \(OC=x\) and \(\angle COH=\theta\). Thus \(CH=x\sin\theta\). Since \(C\) lies on the bisector of \(\angle ABO\), its distances to \(BA\) and \(BO\) are equal. Therefore
\[
1-x=x\sin\theta,
\qquad x(1+\sin\theta)=1.
\]
Here \(1+\sin\theta>0\), so division is valid. Consequently,
\[
OC=\frac{1}{1+\sin\theta},
\]
which is choice D.

methods.label: Divide the radius using side ratios
methods.explanation:
The angle-bisector theorem directly relates the two parts of \(OA\) to sides of triangle \(OAB\). Tangency gives \(OA\perp AB\), so \(\theta\) is acute and
\[
\sin\theta=\frac{AB}{OB}.
\]
Let \(x=OC\). Since \(BC\) is the internal angle bisector, \(0<x<1\) and \(CA=1-x\). The angle-bisector theorem matches \(OC\) with the adjacent side \(OB\), and \(CA\) with \(AB\), giving
\[
\frac{x}{1-x}=\frac{OB}{AB}
=\frac{1}{\sin\theta}.
\]
Both denominators are positive. Cross-multiplication gives \(x\sin\theta=1-x\), hence
\[
OC=x=\frac{1}{1+\sin\theta}.
\]
The denominator is positive because \(\theta\) is acute. The answer is choice D.
methods.levelReason: Uses the internal angle-bisector theorem and a right-triangle sine ratio without additional trigonometric identities.
